texts.preamble: Suresh Kumar Bansal vs . The State (Da) on 28 March, 2023 In The Court Of Sh. Harjyot Singh Bhalla Additional Sessions Judge-04 Patiala House Courts, New Delhi In The Matter Of: Suresh Kumar Bansal Vs. The State (Da) Cnr No. Dlnd01-006206-2016 Criminal Appeal No. : 8667/2016 Cc No. 103/2011 Suresh Kumar Bansal S/o Sh. Suraj Bhan Bansal M/s. Gupta Store, E-192, Naraina Vihar, New Delhi R/o Ba-95, East Shalimar Bagh, New Delhi-110088 .....Appellant Versus The State (Delhi Administration) Pfa Department, A-20, Lawrence Road, Industrial Area, Delhi ...Respondent Date of Institution : 18.07.2016 Date of decision : 28.03.2023 Cr. Appeal No. 8667/2016 Page 1 of 10 Judgment
texts.facts: Brief facts: 2. That on 16.09.2006, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) Sh. Rajendra Kumar Suresh Kumar Bansal vs . The State (Da) on 28 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/117993979/ 1 Bhaskar and Field Assistant (FA) Sh. D.N. Verma under supervision of SDM/LHA Sh. D.S. Gehlot, reached alongwith their staff at the premises of M/s Gupta Store at E-192, Naraina Vihar, New Delhi-110028, where the appellant was found conducting the business of various food articles which are lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption. The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of 'Pepper Black (Kali Mirch) Whole'. Sample of the Kali Mirch was purchased and divided into 3 counterparts and were separated packed, fastened, marked and sealed, as per the provisions of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955. One counterpart of the sample was sent to Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM.LHA. Vide report dated 06.05.2011, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that it contained mineral oil and exceed the prescribed maximum limit of 5.0%. Accordingly, after completion of investigation, sanction under Section 20 of the Act was obtained and the complaint was then filed on 03.06.2011 for violation of Section 2 (ia) (a), (b) & (m) of the PFA Act as well as Section 2 (ix)(d) of PFA Act read with Rule 44-AAA Rules, as punishable under Section 7/16 (1)(a) of PFA Act. 3. The appellant was summoned vide order dated 03.06.2011. An application under Section 13(2) of the Act was filed by the appellant on 18.11.2006 thereby exercising his right to get the second counterpart of the sample analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL). The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent to CFL. The CFL examined the sample and gave Certificate dated 12.07.2011, opining the sample to be not conforming to the standards of Black Pepper (Kali Mirch) Whole as per PFA Rules due to the presence of mineral oil. 4. On the basis of CFL Report, notice of accusation under Section 251 Cr.P.C. was framed against the accused on 22.12.2011 for commission of offence punishable under Section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act, being violation of Section 2(ia)(a) and (m), to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 5. The prosecution examined three witnesses namely, PW-1 FI R.K Bhaskar, PW-2 Sh. D.S. Gehlot (the then SDM/LHA) and PW-3 FA Sh. D.N. Verma. 6. The statement of the accused was recorded u/s 313 Cr.P.C. on 16.09.2015 in which he claimed his innocence. It submitted that the present appeal is liable to be dismissed. Thereafter, the report of the public analyst was prepared on 06.05.2011 i.e. about 56 months after the collection of sample.
texts.arguments: 7. Ld. SPP for the Department has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused has not been able to rebut the findings of the CFL report dated 12.07.2011. It is also submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony. Ld. Counsel for the appellant has firstly stated that in the present case, the sample was lifted on 16.09.2006. Counsel has emphasized that the present case pertain to perishable food article Black Pepper (Kali Mirch) and the same does not have very long shelf life. He has next contented that not only there was delay on this account itself, there was a further delay of almost 1 month in the filing of the complaint. It was only when, after 1 month, the complaint was filed, the accused got an opportunity to get the second sample tested under Section 13 (2) of PFA Act. However, due to the delay caused in lodging of prosecution, such valuable right of the accused can be said to have been clearly defeated, as under no circumstances, Kali Mirch Whole could have been fit for testing/analyzing after such a long period of time. 11. Ld. Counsel has relied upon the decision in State Vs. Vinod Kumar Gupta, 2010 (2) JCC 987, where lodging of prosecution even after 4 months was rejected on the account of delay as it would defeat the right of the accused for getting the sample tested for the second time. 12. Ld. Counsel has, in support of his contention, further relied upon the decision in MCD Vs. Ghisa Ram, Criminal Appeal No. 194/66 in SC of PFA cases 1951-1975 at page 93 and decision in Chanan Lal Vs. State, 1972 PFA Cases 292, as also, Girish Bhai Dahiyabhai Shah Vs. CC Jani, 2009 (2) FAC 194. 13. 18. For this it would be relevant to refer to the provisions of Section 23(1A)(ee) and (hh) which read as follows: "23(1A) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power, such rules may provide for all or any of the following matters, namely:- ............................ (ee) defining the laboratories where samples of articles of food or adulterants may be analysed by public analysts under this act; ....................... (hh) defining the methods of analysis These aspects were considered by the Apex Court in the case of Pepsico India Holdings Pvt. Ltd. vs. Food Inspector & Anr. (2011) 1 SCC (Cri) 8. In the said case, the point raised for consideration was whether in the absence of any prescribed and validated method of analysis u/s 23 (1a) (hh) of the Act, could a prosecution be launched against the appellants based on the reports submitted by the Public Analyst using the method of the Director General of Health Services (DGHS). 24. This judgment of the Apex Court was followed by the Kerala High Court in the case of R. Gopalakrishnan Vs. Food Inspector in Criminal Revision Petition No.671/2002 decided on 17.07.2013. Special Leave Petition against the said judgment was preferred in Supreme Court of India, vide Criminal Appeal No. 2476 of 2014, but the same was dismissed. 25. In a recent judgment of M/s Nestle India Ltd. Vs. the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and Ors. 2015 (2) FAC 56 the Bombay High Court has again followed the Pepsico case (supra) to observe that in the absence of designated laboratories and validated methods of analysis, the reports of the Public Analyst and the Director, CFL, cannot be relied upon. 26. Reliance is also placed upon the decision of the Hon'ble Kerala High Court in Mohanan P. & Others Vs. State of Kerala and Another, Crl. Rev. P.No. 66 of 2011, decided on 25th November, 2021 where the earlier decision in R. Gopalakrishnan (supra) has again been followed. 28. In Dhian Singh Vs. Municipal Board Saharanpur, AIR 1970 SC 318, the Hon'ble Supreme Court was of the view that the report of the PA need not contain the mode or particular of analysis nor the test applied. The Suresh Kumar Bansal vs . The State (Da) on 28 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/117993979/ The decision in Dhian Singh (Supra), most respectfully, would cease to be the applicable law on the aspect in view of the specific legislative mandate introduced by way of amendment.
